centralClaim: A US military operation against a Chinese ship was aborted after officials found the intelligence report behind it had been generated with an AI chatbot that inaccurately identified the ship's cargo.
sendTest: Des avions militaires américains étaient déjà en vol pour arraisonner un navire chinois. Le renseignement venait d'un chatbot, et il était faux.

corroboration.quote: It was only just before the planned operation that officials dug deeper into the report put together by a special operations command analyst and found it had been generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) - and that a chatbot the analyst had used inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.

Military aircraft were already in the air this spring when U.S. officials made an alarming discovery: The intelligence driving an armed operation against a Chinese vessel had been hallucinated by an AI chatbot.

caption:
Des avions militaires étaient déjà en l'air. Le renseignement qui les envoyait venait d'un chatbot.

CNN révèle qu'une opération armée contre un navire chinois a été annulée au dernier moment, ce printemps. Le rapport disait que le bateau transportait des composants d'un programme d'arme nucléaire. Il avait été fabriqué avec une intelligence artificielle, et le chatbot s'était trompé sur la cargaison.

Comment c'est arrivé. Un analyste du commandement des opérations spéciales a demandé à un chatbot de fusionner des données publiques avec du renseignement électronique secret. Puis il a redemandé à l'IA de mettre le résultat en forme, dans le format de rapport auquel les officiers font confiance, et il l'a diffusé.

Le détail qui n'est pas dans la vidéo. Personne ne sait quel outil c'était. CNN écrit qu'on ignore s'il s'agissait d'un chatbot du commerce ou d'un produit du gouvernement, et un ancien haut responsable résume les outils internes comme des copies du commerce avec du rouge à lèvres dessus.

Ce qui coince. Une source dit à CNN que ce genre d'erreur n'est pas un cas isolé dans la communauté du renseignement, et qu'il n'existe aucune norme commune pour vérifier ce que ces outils produisent.

Jake Steckler, chercheur à GovAI et ancien officier de l'armée américaine, dit à TechCrunch qu'il y a des conséquences de vie ou de mort attachées à ces décisions.

captionEvidence.quote: The intelligence report, circulated across the US military this spring in the midst of the war with Iran, immediately set off alarm bells: A Chinese ship in the Middle East was transporting components of a nuclear weapons program.

It was only just before the planned operation that officials dug deeper into the report put together by a special operations command analyst and found it had been generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) - and that a chatbot the analyst had used inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.
The bot fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings and reached its fateful conclusion about the material the ship was carrying.
The analyst then used AI again to package the findings into a standard intelligence report - the kind that is trusted by military officials - and disseminated it.
It was not clear whether the chatbot was a commercially available one or a US government product.
"The internal tools are mostly just copies of the commercial stuff wearing lipstick," a former senior US official familiar with the AI systems used by military and intelligence analysts.

The kind of "hallucination" that the tool used by the analyst in this case conjured has not been an isolated incident across the intelligence community since these tools began proliferating across government, according to one of the sources.
There's no one set of standards for how the US verifies the information generated by these tools.
"It's important for service members to understand the uncertainty inherent to LLMs," said Jake Steckler, research scholar at GovAI and veteran U.S. Army officer, in a written response to TechCrunch.
There are life and death consequences for those decisions.
One source told CNN that the "hallucination" was part of a trend in the U.S. military, not an isolated incident.
